turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，伦尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's absolutely my pleasure. I've heard so many great things about you from so many people. I think you're friends with a lot of guests that have been on this podcast. turns.zh: 非常荣幸能与你交流。我听过很多人对你的赞誉，知道你和很多做客过这个播客的嘉宾都是朋友。让我觉得你非常有趣且值得尊敬的地方在于，你曾在许多优秀的公司工作，职业生涯成就斐然，但却几乎不发推特，没有通讯稿，在领英上动态也很少。甚至我找不到你上过播客的任何证据，唯一能证明你存在的可能就是你的YouTube频道——里面全是卡丁车、孩子，还有人们祝你生日快乐的内容。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Oh gosh, I should go monitor that. I forgot about that.
turns.zh: 天哪，我得去看看那个频道了。我都忘了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You might want to go find it now.
turns.zh: 你现在最好去找找看。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah that's funny. Yeah, it's funny. I think about that a lot, like am I doing something wrong? Should I be putting more effort in that? I mean, it's funny that you mentioned newsletter. I spend a lot of time with the Substack team's. I've been a very active advisor there. The team is fantastic by the way. And I think about it. Am I doing something wrong in my career by not doing that? But just to be honest, it doesn't come authentically to me. It doesn't come naturally to me. I get really focused on the thing that I'm working on and get really deep in the thing that I am working on and I have a hard time kind of multitasking a lot outside of that to be totally honest. The way that I kind of get to know the industry and other teams or whatnot is just through working with people. (00:05:58): I'm not a very big networker. I'm not saying that there's anything wrong with that. I wish I were better at that. I get to know people by doing work with them, by helping them. And it doesn't necessarily scale in the same way that Twitter does, but it's served me well so far and it's more kind of authentic and it's what comes more natural to me. And so that's how I do it. So I'm doing a lot of coffees. I'm meeting people that way. I'm not doing a lot of tweeting or writing of newsletters. Maybe one day, but that's not me today.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，是啊，这挺有趣的。我经常思考这个问题——我是不是做错了什么？是不是应该在这方面多下功夫？说到通讯稿，你提到这个让我挺感兴趣的。我和Substack团队合作了很久，一直是他们的活跃顾问。顺便说一句，他们团队非常棒。我也思考过这个问题——我不做通讯稿，在职业生涯中是不是错过了什么机会？但说实话，这对我来说不太自然。它不符合我的真实风格。我会全身心投入到手头的工作中，深入钻研项目，说实话，要我同时处理很多其他事情太难了。我了解行业、其他团队等信息的方式，就是通过与人合作。（00:05:58）我不擅长社交。虽然我不否认社交也有其价值，但对我来说，工作更重要。这更符合我的天性。所以我主要通过喝咖啡来社交，通过帮助他人来认识新人。可能未来会尝试推特或通讯稿，但现在还不是时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think this is an awesome example of you can be incredibly successful as a product manager and as anyone in tech not investing time posting online. I am going to incriminate myself here, but I feel like the advice I always share with people is the best people are not spending time tweeting and talking online and sharing on LinkedIn. They're just doing the work. They don't have time for that sort of thing. And I think you're a great example of that. Is there anything along those lines that you share with folks that are just like, "Hey, should I be investing time here?"
turns.zh: 这就是一个绝佳的例子，说明作为产品经理或科技行业从业者，不必把时间花在网络平台上。说实话，我自己也有过类似经历。我总是告诉别人：最优秀的人不花时间在推特、领英上社交，他们只专注于工作。他们没有时间做这些事。而你就是一个很好的例子。对于那些纠结“我是否该在这些平台上投入时间”的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I think everyone can chart their own path and has a way that is sort of authentic to them and leans on their strengths. What I often coach people is, do what you like. You're generally going to be a lot better at the things that really fill you up that really get you excited. Life is short. There's so many things to be doing out there. We're so lucky. The number of interesting waves of technology that I've experienced, it just makes me feel like it's going to keep happening for a long time. We're very fortunate to be born in the time that we are and have the opportunities that we are. So why spend your time doing something that doesn't feel good because you think that it might lead to some success, where if you lean on what's authentic to you and what makes you happy, chances are you're going to be one of the best people at those things?
turns.zh: 我认为每个人都能规划自己的道路，找到一条既忠实于自我、又能发挥自身优势的道路。我经常给人们的建议是，去做你喜欢的事。通常来说，当你热爱并充满激情去做某件事时，你会表现得更出色。人生短暂，世间有太多值得尝试的事。我们何其幸运。我亲历了多波科技浪潮，这让我深信这种创新势头还将持续很久。我们生于这个时代，得天独厚地拥有诸多机遇。何必为了追求所谓的成功而去做自己不喜欢的事呢？若能坚守本心、追随快乐，成功往往水到渠成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. And I think it's so important. I think there's a lot of pressure on people too. "I need to do this, I need to do that."
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这种建议，而且觉得它至关重要。如今人们承受着太多压力，总被要求“必须做这个，必须做那个”。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "I need to tweet, I need to share content to be successful." This comes up a lot in this podcast, that the more you could just stick close to what gives you energy and what you enjoy doing, oftentimes that leads to things you wouldn't expect in a lot of success. (00:08:07): Speaking of that, looking at your career arc, I noticed a really interesting pattern and a really diverse set of experiences. So just kind of talking through places you've been. At Facebook, you worked on 0 to 1 stuff. At YouTube, the way I see it as you almost went from -1 to 1. At Thumbtack, it looks like you went from 1 to -1 and then back to 1. So it's like a really unique turnaround story. And then with Grammarly it feels like it's like, I don't know, 1 or I don't know, 5 to 100, or wherever you end up taking it. So I thought it'd be fun to talk through each of these experiences because they're such unique approaches or such unique experiences and see what lessons and wisdom we can extract from your journey.
turns.zh: “必须发推文，必须分享内容才能成功。”这个话题在播客中反复出现——若能紧紧抓住能激发你能量、让你享受其中的事物，成功往往超出你的想象。（00:08:07）：说到这，回顾你的职业生涯，我注意到一个非常有趣的模式和丰富多样的经历。就谈谈你走过的路吧。在Facebook，你参与了从0到1的创新；在YouTube，在我看来你几乎是从-1到1的逆袭；在Thumbtack，似乎是从1到-1再回归1。这样的逆袭故事实属罕见。再到Grammarly，感觉就像……我不知道，从1到5到100，或者最终达到何种高度。于是我觉得回顾这些经历会很有趣，因为它们都是独特的策略或非凡的历程，或许能从中提炼出宝贵的经验与智慧。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: That sounds great. Yeah.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, sweet. So I'm thinking reverse chronologically, we start with YouTube, which the way I see it is it's kind of -1 to 1. When you join, my understanding is YouTube was losing a lot of money. When you left, they were not losing money. And I was actually just looking, they're valued apparently at $200 billion today, YouTube as a business. I know you haven't been there for a while, but great work. What lessons did you take away from that journey? What stories come to mind from that part of your career that might be helpful to people?
turns.zh: 好的，太好了。那我打算按时间顺序来聊起——从YouTube开始。在我看来，YouTube当时几乎是-1到1的局面。你加入时，YouTube亏损严重；你离开时，已经实现了盈亏平衡。我刚查了一下，如今YouTube作为一家企业估值高达2000亿美元。虽然你已经离开很久了，但还是要称赞你的出色贡献。从这段经历中，你收获了哪些教训？职业生涯中有没有哪些故事能给人们带来启发？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Maybe first to start looking with why hop around these experiences. I always tell people I feel like I'm an IC trapped in a manager's body sometimes. Fundamentally, I like to build, that's why I do this. I like to make things. And so sometimes the more fun way to make things is to start something and sometimes the better way to make things in the situation that I'm in is to try to support teams and lead through teams. (00:09:50): And so I joined YouTube through an acquisition of a company I started. In the beginning, what I was doing there is just rebuilding that product on Google infrastructure and for YouTube customers. And maybe the first lesson was actually to look around at what the rest of the team was doing and be really honest and open about the relative priority of the thing that you're working on even if it might lead to your project getting canceled. (00:10:26): So one of the things that I remember doing really on is actually talking to the leadership team and being like, "I don't think we should be putting 50 engineers on this project. Looking at the rest of the roadmap and the rest of the priorities, excuse me, I think this team would likely be better served elsewhere." Even though that was likely negotiating my way out of a job in month three, I don't know, I kind of felt like that was the right thing for the team and for the business. (00:10:57): And then that started a very interesting journey because from there, basically the leadership was like, "You're right. We're going to wind that down and build some of those features into the existing product. And now you, you come and lead this focus area, we're calling the creator focus area." So I went from basically rebuilding the product that our startup had built to leading one of the three focus areas at YouTube. There was the viewer team, the creator team, and the advertiser team. And Hunter Walk, who's amazing, was leading the viewer team. And Shishir Mehrotra, who's also very amazing, was leading the advertising team.
turns.zh:
或许首先要探讨一下为何频繁切换这些工作经历。我常对人们说，有时我感觉自己像个被困在管理者身体里的工程师。说到底，我热爱创造，这也是我从事这份工作的初衷。我喜欢动手做事。因此，有时以创新思维开创新事物会更有趣；而在当前环境下，通过团队赋能、以身作则来支持团队成长或许才是更明智的选择。（00:09:50）  

我曾通过收购一家自己创办的公司加入YouTube。最初，我致力于将该产品迁移至谷歌基础设施并面向YouTube用户优化服务。这里的首要经验在于：要审视团队其他成员的工作方向，并坦诚评估自己所负责项目的优先级——即便这可能意味着项目被叫停。（00:10:26）  

我记得最引人注目的一次行动，是向领导团队直言：“我认为我们不应为这个项目投入50名工程师。综合路线图与其他优先事项来看，恕我直言，这个团队或许能在其他领域创造更大价值。” 尽管这相当于在入职第三个月就为自己争取脱身机会，但我坚信这对团队和业务都是正确的选择。（00:10:57）  

此后便开启了一段有趣的旅程。领导层认可了我的观点，决定暂停该项目，将相关功能整合至现有产品中。随即，我被委以重任，负责领导YouTube的三大核心业务领域之一——创作者专注区。其他两个团队分别由Hunter Walk（杰出人才）和Shishir Mehrotra（同样卓越的领导者）负责，分别负责观众体验和广告业务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an alumni community.
turns.zh: 这真是一个充满前辈智慧的社区。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: There was me. I was sort of like 29-year-old startupy guy working with these guys who were awesome. And YouTube in general, and continues to be, an incredible team. And so I think that was a first really good lesson. That in the right organizations, even in large organizations, advocate for what's best for the team, advocate for what's best for the organization even if that means that it puts you at a particular difficult moment. If it is a healthy team that rewards those sorts of decisions and actions, good things will happen. If it's not, that's good to know too. That's good to know early. So that's one thing that comes to mind. (00:12:32): Maybe one other I would say atypical career choice that I made shortly thereafter is then when I was put in that role, I really struggled in that role. I was reporting to the CEO at the time, a guy named Salar Kamangar, who's also awesome, Google's 6th employee and just learned a ton from him, like an incredible strategic thinker. But he was asking me questions that I felt like they were from a different planet. I was like, I didn't know what they meant and he just thought in a different way, a different level or different scale and that's still something that I was learning. Eventually I figured it out, but I was really struggling in that moment. I had a really good relationship with both Hunter and Shishir and they really helped me through that. And eventually, I went to Salar and said, "Hey, I think I should actually report to Hunter. I think this would work better if we kind of combined the organizations this way and then we divided and conquered this way." (00:13:41): And again, very atypical, no one has ever come to me in my career and said, "I would like you to layer me in this other person." But in that moment I was just like, "This is how I will do better work. This is how I will get better support. I will be happier and more productive and it'll be better for the team." And you know what? For me anyway, I was right. We made that change. Hunter was a fantastic manager and support at YouTube. I learned a ton, grew a lot. And then eventually when he moved on, Shishir took over the organization and then I moved into the viewer part of the organization, which is where I spent the rest of my time there, which was leading and supporting the viewer PM team at YouTube.
turns.zh: 当时的我29岁，是个初出茅庐的创业者，与那些才华横溢的同事共事。而YouTube整个团队，过去是、现在依然是一支超凡的团队。所以我认为这是一个非常宝贵的启示：在合适的组织里，即便是大型机构，只要你能为团队、为组织的最大利益发声，即便这意味着你会面临短期的挑战，只要团队足够健康，奖励这种决策与行动的机制到位，好事就会发生。若情况相反，尽早察觉也未尝不可。这就是我首先领悟到的道理。（00:12:32）：接下来，我想说另一个非典型职业选择——在接手那个角色后，我深陷困境。当时我的上司是Salar Kamangar，他同样才华出众，作为谷歌第六位员工，我从他身上学到了许多战略思维。但他提的问题有时让我觉得天外来客，我根本不明白他的意思。后来我才意识到，他思考问题的维度、层次和规模与我完全不同，这仍是我需要学习的地方。最终我找到解决方案，但当时确实很煎熬。我与Hunter和Shishir关系融洽，他们帮我渡过难关。最后我找到Salar，提议："我认为我应该向Hunter汇报工作。若能整合两个团队、各司其职，效果会更好。"（00:13:41）：这再次打破常规——职业生涯中从未有人主动提出"把我归入其他团队"。但那一刻我坚信："这样才能更好地开展工作，获得支持，提高效率，最终造福团队。"事实证明我的选择正确。Hunter成为YouTube卓越的管理者，带给我诸多启发。后来Shishir接管团队后，我转入观众业务部门，在那里度过剩余时光，负责YouTube的观众产品管理团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These stories are amazing. It connects to your point that you're kind of an, I see, an inner child I see, where you keep trying to kill your career by accident. Like, "Now, let's kill this project I'm working on. I'm going to demote myself a little bit." But clearly it's worked out. Is there anything that you saw that gave you that confidence that, "This is actually going to be okay"? Because again, people don't normally think this is how you get ahead in your career, is you kill your team and you layer yourself.
turns.zh: 这些故事太精彩了。这让我联想到你提到的观点——你内心仿佛有个孩子，总在不经意间自毁前程。比如："现在，让我毁掉手头的项目。我要把自己降职一级。" 但显然最终都迎来了转机。是否有某个瞬间让你坚定信心："这事儿其实没问题"？毕竟大多数人不会认为自毁团队、架空上司是晋升之道。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think having a broader view of the company strategy, having an instinct for what we should be doing and why and how I might prioritize all of these investments if I were given the opportunity to do that, I think internalizing that and understanding that and then trying to align whatever is under your influence towards that overall goal is very helpful and made me feel like, "I'm pretty confident this is going to be okay because it will lead to better results for the organization given what we're trying to do. And so as long as I'm trying to push decisions or actions that actually lead to better results, if it's a healthy culture and organization, I should be okay." (00:15:47): I think that the other thing is, just over the years, I got extremely lucky. The first job that I got out of school was an incredible group of people and it gave me a nose for talent. It gave me a nose for what great feels like and what a high functioning team feels like. It's hard to know that without experiencing that. And so in the moments, YouTube was also one of those teams, Grammarly is one of those teams, Thumbtack was one of those teams. Being able to sniff that out when you're trying to choose the next team is very important. But I think that's another thing that gave me confidence. I learned these people well enough, Hunter, Shishir, et cetera, to have the instinct that the right thing will happen, like this will be better for me and the broader team.
turns.zh:
是的，我觉得要对公司的战略有更宏观的理解，要有直觉去判断我们应该做什么、为什么要做，以及如果有机会的话，我会如何优先安排这些投资项目。把这些道理内化并理解后，再努力让在自己影响范围内的所有事务都朝着那个总体目标迈进，这非常有帮助。它让我觉得：“我很有信心这会没问题，因为这将为我们正在努力达成的目标带来更好的结果。只要我努力推动那些能带来更好结果的决策或行动，如果公司文化和组织架构良好，事情应该就不会出错。”  
（00:15:47）：另外，这些年来我也非常幸运。毕业后得到的第一份工作团队极其出色，他们让我对人才有了敏锐的洞察力。让我明白了什么是优秀的团队，什么是高效运作的团队。没有亲身经历过这些，很难理解其中的奥秘。YouTube、Grammarly、Thumbtack等团队都是这样的例子。在选择下一支团队时，能敏锐地识别出这些特质非常重要。但我认为这也是让我充满信心的另一个原因。我对Hunter、Shishir等人有了足够深入的了解，养成了这样的直觉：正确的决策终将水到渠成，对我个人和整个团队都更有利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the key there is just you have to trust that the team around you is good enough, that you're not going to be pushed off into a corner. I think you made a really profound point here that a lot of people don't get about the job of a product leader and a product manager, that a big part of your job is to think about what is best for the business and work backwards from that. Not necessarily what's the best thing for the user is the highest priority, not necessarily what's the best thing for my team and how do I hit the goals that I'm obsessed with. It's what is going to be best for the business broadly and then make decisions there. Is there anything more you can say there about just how powerful that is as a way of thinking about prioritization and decisions as a product manager?
turns.zh: 明白了。关键在于你必须相信身边的团队足够优秀，不会把你晾在一边。我觉得你在这里提出了一个深刻的观点——很多产品负责人和产品经理都忽视了这一点：你的核心职责是从业务角度出发，逆向推导决策。用户需求未必是首要任务，团队需求也未必是重中之重，真正关键的是要考虑对整个业务最有利的方向，再据此制定决策。作为产品经理，在优先级排序和决策制定方面，这种宏观视角的力量有多大？你能否再深入谈谈？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I mean, I think ideally, things that are best for the customer, there's high overlap with that with things that are best for the business, but not always, right? And I think figuring out some principles that help guide those sorts of conflicts can be really, really helpful. At Thumbtack, we had principles about which sides of the marketplace we wanted to serve in which order and when we serve Thumbtack. So it was customers first, pros second, and then Thumbtack last. And that's actually the first two... Saying Thumbtack last is the easy thing to say. Actually doing it in action I think is a very different thing. But that first one of like, should we... Especially when you're starting a marketplace, as you know well, Lenny, supply is so critical. Many marketplaces live and die by the quality and liquidity and supply. And so why would you focus on customers first and the Thumbtack perspective and supply are the pros, the people that you hire? (00:18:41): Well, we always just felt that what the pros need from us is more customers. What the pros need from us is high quality customers. And so if we really try to make a great customer experience that attracts more customers, helps them find the right pros, provides the highest quality customers, then that will therefore be better for the pros. And so that's how we should prioritize. If we do those things right, then the business will benefit, right? And so doing things like raising prices because we think it's good for the business, even though it causes liquidity issues in the marketplace might be a little bit of a local maxima, locally optimizing rather than globally optimizing. So I think sometimes in these sorts of questions, trying to establish some set of guiding principles that help navigate some of these more ambiguous or thorny questions can be really helpful.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个很棒的问题。我觉得理想情况下，对客户最有利的事情，往往也与对企业最有利的事情高度重叠，但并非总是如此，对吧？我认为制定一些原则来指导这类冲突，是非常有帮助的。在Thumbtack，我们有一些原则，关于我们想以何种顺序服务市场中的哪些群体，以及何时为Thumbtack服务。所以是先服务客户，再服务从业者，最后服务Thumbtack本身。这实际上是前两个原则……说先服务Thumbtack本身倒是容易，但真正在行动中做到却截然不同。但第一个原则是，比如，我们是否应该……尤其是当你刚创立一个市场平台时，正如你所知，Lenny，供应是至关重要的。许多市场平台的兴衰取决于供应的质量和流动性。那么，为什么要先关注客户，再关注Thumbtack的视角，最后才是供应方——即你雇佣的从业者呢？（00:18:41） 嗯，我们一直觉得从业者需要我们提供更多客户。他们需要高质量的客户。所以如果我们能真正打造吸引更多客户、帮助他们找到合适从业者、提供最高质量客户的优质客户体验，那么这对从业者来说自然更好。所以这就是我们的优先次序。如果我们把这些事情做好，业务自然会受益，对吧？所以像因为认为有利于业务而提高价格这样的做法，尽管可能会导致市场流动性问题，但可能只是局部的优化，而非全局最优。所以我认为在面对这类问题时，试图建立一套指导原则来帮助应对这些更模糊或棘手的问题，确实很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to circle back to this first point you made, an experience you had convincing people that your first project shouldn't be something you work on. How long do you stick with something that isn't going well and then decide, "Okay, let's convince people this is something I should move on from," versus you don't want to give up on a project quickly, you want to give it a shot?
turns.zh: 我想回过头来谈谈你提到的第一个观点，即你曾说服别人你的第一个项目不应该是你亲自操刀的。对于进展不顺利的事情，你会坚持多久，然后决定“好吧，让我们说服别人我应该放弃这个项目”？还是说你不想轻易放弃一个项目，而是想再努力一把？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I mean, look, I don't know that it's a perfect answer, but I think the reality is just that what kills most projects most early companies is stamina. And I think that we all need to work on being more resilient about kind of like, I remember at Thumbtack, Marco, the CEO, we used to say that it feels like we're running uphill and chewing glass, and you're kind of like, "That's right, we want to do that. That's good for us. Take our medicine." So you want to practice that sort of resiliency. But ultimately, I think that what starts to happen is you start to lose the stamina and you're just not bringing your best self to the situation. (00:20:42): And so many of these things that are so high ambiguity where you don't know exactly what to build or you don't know exactly, you're not getting the signal you need or the feedback you need to be able to hone it in and know that you're doing something well. They require just an ungodly level of faith and stamina. And so that's sort of what I look to. When you see a team that is motivated, that is building something like they're really excited about, I mean just the inertia, the quality, it's like a whole different game where when you see a team that's sort of down and out and they've really been hitting their head against the wall for a long time, sometimes they just need a change of scene, a change of pace, and they get to a much better situation. So my honest answer is, yeah, it's the, when do you run out of steam is usually the question. I think that happens usually like in the startup case, a lot of times before you run out money or these other things.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，你看，我不知道这是否是个完美的答案，但我认为现实情况是，大多数项目和早期公司之所以夭折，最主要的原因在于缺乏耐力。我们都需要努力变得更具韧性。比如，我记得在Thumbtack时，首席执行官马可常说感觉自己在逆水行舟、吃力不讨好，但你会想：“没错，我们就该这样做。这对我们有益。吃点苦头吧。”所以你得锻炼这种韧性。但最终，耐力会被消耗殆尽，你无法在困境中发挥出最佳状态。（00:20:42）很多高不确定性的项目，比如你不确定该开发什么功能，或者得不到所需的反馈来调整方向，这些都需要超乎寻常的信念和耐力。所以这正是我所看重的。当你看到一个团队充满激情，专注于令他们兴奋不已的项目时，那种势不可挡的动力和高品质表现，简直是天壤之别。相反，当团队陷入低谷、长期碰壁时，他们有时只需要换个环境、调整节奏，就能迎来质的转变。所以我的坦诚回答是，嗯，通常问题在于你何时会精疲力竭。在创业环境中，这种情况常在资金告急或其他危机出现前就悄然发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've talked about Thumbtack a couple of times now, so let's talk about that. I love this description of running a pill, chewing glass. My understanding is when you joined, things were going well, and then things started to go much less well, and then you helped turn things around. Talk about that part of your journey and what you learned from that time.
turns.zh: 我们已经多次提到Thumbtack了，现在就来聊聊这个案例。我特别喜欢“吃力不讨好”的比喻。我的理解是，你加入时一切顺利，但后来情况急转直下，而你成功扭转了局面。能否谈谈这段经历，以及你从中获得的启发？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, sure. Again, really fantastic team and really strong founders. That company was just on the bleeding edge of things like SEO and growing by SEO. It was one of the best organizations that are driving growth through that channel. But I think a thing that I learned really early, which Lenny with your background you probably know as well, SEO is a sort of a live by the sword, die by the sword channel of growth. I think that one channel growth company is always a no-no. And so that's a little bit of what we had at Thumbtack. (00:22:44): So it was funny, because I remember when I joined and Marco and I had an agreement where it's like, "Okay, I'm going to do my three months of onboarding, listening to our new leader inheriting a team." I've always gotten advice that that's what you should do. And Marco being an entrepreneur and a hard running founder is like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah. Sure, sure." And then a month in, it's like, "All right, we got to run 2024 planning. Go." Or not 2024, sorry, at the time it was. And yeah, in the early days when I was there, Thumbtack was seeing triple digit growth. Then we had a couple SEO hits that got us down to double-digit growth. And then not too long after that, we were actually, for the first time in the company's history, seeing negative year-over-year growth and Google was just really coming down on our category as we were, by the way, trying to rebuild the whole product and change the monetization model and everything in between. (00:23:50): So it was a really a tough moment of how much do we kind of spend to reinforce the old model while we're sort of building the new model, kind of changing the engine while the plane is flying. I think I remember in a board meeting, once we kind of turned that around and over time and also the new model really started to show legs and really started to work, one of the board members, Brian Schreier at Sequoia, said it was the prettiest smile graph that he had ever, ever seen. It was obviously a really proud moment there. (00:24:24): But I think that the thing that I took away from that, which I tell PMs quite a bit, is growth masks all problems. You don't really have a, I think, true understanding of what is working well and what is not working well when you have incredible growth. YouTube was a great example of that. And at Thumbtac, it had incredible growth for quite some time, but it was essentially burning through a lot of demand. It was just dropping a lot of demand on the floor because there wasn't sufficient liquidity on the supply side to really meet that demand. The team knew and was trying to work on that problem, but it wasn't as urgent or high priority because you're having triple digit growth. What's wrong? Everything's going great, right? (00:25:11): And then the moment growth starts to slow or certainly when growth starts to be negative, all of a sudden the tenor in the organization really changes and you start looking at things very differently and trying to understand what's actually going on. And so I think it's actually a very healthy thing for businesses to go through as they turn into long-term sustainable businesses to have those sorts of moments, because I think otherwise it's just really challenging to identify where the true issues are. And I think as a PM, if you've only ever worked on things that grow and you've never felt the other side of that and how to help turn that around with your team, I think you lose a lot in your career if you don't experience that. (00:25:58): I'm kind of naturally paranoid. And especially as I manage growth, I often look at things and ask myself like, "Okay, what do I do right now if it went negative? How would I prioritize things if it went negative?" Having gone through that experience, I just look at things in a different way of urgency. I look at things at different levels of priority having gone through that experience.
turns.zh:
是的，当然。再次强调，这是一个非常出色的团队，创始人也非常强大。那家公司在SEO和通过SEO实现增长方面走在了前沿。它是通过这个渠道推动增长的最佳组织之一。但我很早就意识到一点——以伦尼（Lenny）的背景，你可能也深有体会——SEO这种增长渠道就像"成也萧何，败也萧何"。任何一家单一渠道增长型公司都注定行不通。这正是Thumbtack早期遇到的困境。（00:22:44）：说起来挺有趣的，我记得刚加入公司时，马可（Marco）和我达成了一个协议："好的，我会进行为期三个月的入职培训，听取新任领导如何接手团队。"我一直听说新人应该这么做。但马可作为创业者和高效的创始人，总是会说："是啊，是啊，是啊。当然，当然。"结果一个月后，他就说："好吧，我们要开始规划2024年的策略。行动起来。"或者不是2024年，当时是另外一个年份。早期Thumbtack的增长率达到了三位数，但随后遭遇了几次SEO打击，增长率降至两位数。不久之后，公司历史上首次出现同比负增长，而谷歌正严厉打击我们的行业类别。与此同时，我们正试图重建整个产品、改变盈利模式等一系列改革。（00:23:50）：那真是一个艰难的时刻：在构建新模式的同时，我们还要维持旧模式吗？这就像在飞机飞行时更换引擎。我记得在一次董事会会议上，当我们扭转局面后，随着新模式逐渐成效显著，红杉资本的布莱恩·施雷尔（Brian Schreier）说，这是他见过最漂亮的增长曲线图。这无疑是一个值得骄傲的时刻。（00:24:24）：但我从中领悟到的一点——我经常和产品经理们分享——增长会掩盖所有问题。当增长率极高时，你很难真正理解哪些方面做得好，哪些方面做得不好。YouTube就是一个很好的例子。Thumbtack也曾长期保持惊人的增长，但本质上是在大量消耗需求，因为供应端没有足够的流动性来满足这些需求。团队知道并试图解决这个问题，但由于增长率极高，问题并没有被视为紧急或高优先级。出什么问题了？一切都很顺利，对吧？（00:25:11）：但当增长开始放缓，特别是当增长率转为负值时，组织内部的氛围会突然改变，你会以完全不同的视角审视问题，试图理解实际情况。因此，我认为对于企业来说，当它们发展为长期可持续的业务时，经历这样的阶段实际上是件好事，因为否则很难识别出真正的问题所在。作为产品经理，如果你只参与过增长型项目，从未体验过失败和带领团队扭转局面的过程，我认为你的职业生涯会因此蒙受损失。（00:25:58）：我天生就有些多疑。尤其是当我管理团队时。
关于成长，我常常审视事物并自问：“好吧，如果情况变得不利，我现在该怎么做？如果事态恶化，我该如何分清轻重缓急？”经历过那些挫折后，我看待事物的方式变得更加紧迫，也能在不同层面区分事情的优先级了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With this Thumbtack story, I think it's rare that a business gets the smile graph that you described, this prettiest smile graph that this board member has ever seen. I think that is rarely the case. Usually, it doesn't come back up. Can you share what you did to help Thumbtack turn things around? I know it's very particular to Thumbtack in the business, but just anything there that would be useful to people?
turns.zh: 关于Thumbtack的这个案例，我觉得一家企业能获得你所描述的这种“微笑曲线”——这种董事会成员见过的最完美的微笑曲线——实在难得。我认为这种情况实属罕见。通常情况下，曲线并不会出现如此显著的回升。你能否分享一下是如何帮助Thumbtack扭转局面的？我知道这对Thumbtack的业务模式而言非常独特，但其中是否有一些经验教训能对其他人有所启发？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Sure. First of all, this is very much the team. It's not just things that I did. So I mean, first was turning on multiple channels of growth. Up until then, Thumbtack had tried and stopped paid channels, other organic channels like referrals, all of the typical things. And so, we just went back to first principles on a lot of that and also just kind of reformed a team around that and basically got an amazing team together. One of them, Whitney Steele is running marketing at Descript now. Another one, David Schein is running a product at HIMSS. But basically I went back to first principles on some of those growth channels and experiment on our way to much, much better results. (00:27:42): I think that one of the things that we were doing incorrectly at Thumbtack is Thumbtack is actually a marketplace that is actually made up of thousands of marketplaces, right? Like DJs in Philadelphia is one marketplace, DJs in Atlanta is another marketplace, contractors in Sonoma is another marketplace. And then Thumbtack is obviously the container of all of those marketplaces. I think we were just bifurcating our targeting and our growth efforts a little too narrowly, assuming we had to grow in that way market by market rather than targeting more broadly, providing the more aggregate data to Google and others, and then optimizing from there. The fact that we already had really good showing in SEO and really good patriarch and SEO helped to bolster things like SEM and then eventually Facebook as well. (00:28:40): Those were kind of the growth levers, but the core issue with the Thumbtack product was that it was just a very high friction customer experience that really left customers waiting. So the way that Thumbtack worked basically was a customer would find them through a search query, they would come in and they would answer a number of questions about the job they needed done, and then Thumbtack would say, "Okay, great, we'll get back to you in 24 hours." And this is a modern day experience, right? (00:29:17): And then what Thumbtack would do is they would take that job and they would federate it out to as many of the pros that might match the criteria, and then the pros would pay to quote to show up as a potential provider for that job. Now, I don't want to take anything away from that team because that worked phenomenally well for a really long time. And actually it's a perfect case study in like, "|Just do the scrappy thing that works to grow." And they did that very well, but the stage and size of the business when I joined it had kind of outgrown that. And the team knew that. That's obviously a very high friction experience. The idea that the customer, they're super excited, they want to hire someone, and at that moment you'd be like, "Cool, talk to you soon," not the best experience. (00:30:06): And the fact that you're asking your supply to put up money to even show up to customers in the first place, well, what the customers want to see is the supply. Like, "Tell me who I can hire." Also, a lot of friction on that side and also in some cases some unfair revenue on that side because if folks are paying to be seen and maybe they're looked at, but there's not really high intent, then they're not going to get the customers they want, they're going to be spending revenue, they're not going to be getting revenue back. It turns into just a bad loop obviously. (00:30:40): So the main thing we did is to rebuild that whole loop, change the monetization model, build a system where essentially pros could provide instant quotes. Lenny, I'm sure from Airbnb, this is very familiar, the move from request to book to instant booking. It was a very similar thing in a different kind of category of service and supply obviously. But that shift and doing that shift across those thousands of marketplaces and then finding the right friction point for monetization and when and what to charge people for and all of that change, that is what really, at its core, turned the growth engine around at Thumbtack. And it's just a real testament to those founders that they believe that, saw that, and were willing to run a pill and chew glass to get to that point. I don't know the details of the business anymore. And if I did, I wouldn't speak to it. But from what I hear, things are going well, so I think that that served the company well.
turns.zh:
好的。首先，这主要得归功于整个团队的努力。这不是我一个人就能做到的。比如，我们首先重新启用了多种增长渠道。在此之前，Thumbtack曾尝试过付费推广渠道，但后来放弃了。还有其他自然增长渠道，比如推荐引流等常规手段。但我们回归到增长策略的基本原理，重组团队，最终组建了一支卓越的团队。其中一位成员惠特尼·斯蒂尔现在负责Descript的市场营销，另一位大卫·沙因则在HIMSS负责产品开发。我们重新审视了这些增长渠道，并通过实验取得了显著成效。（00:27:42） 我认为Thumbtack之前在策略上存在一些误区。Thumbtack实际上是由数千个细分市场组成的平台，比如费城的DJ服务市场、亚特兰大的DJ服务市场、索诺玛的承包商市场等等。Thumbtack本身就是这些细分市场的集合体。我们之前把目标市场和增长策略割裂得太厉害，错误地认为必须逐个市场推进，而不是通过更广泛的数据收集来优化。比如，我们SEO和SEM方面做得很好，甚至Facebook推广也取得了成效。（00:28:40） 这些都是增长的关键点，但Thumbtack产品最核心的问题在于用户体验的低效和等待时间过长。Thumbtack的运作模式是，用户通过搜索关键词找到平台，回答一系列需求问题，平台会回复“好的，24小时内给您答复”。这在今天看来很普通，但当时的用户体验确实存在严重问题。（00:29:17） 接下来，Thumbtack会将这些需求推送给符合条件的专业服务商，服务商需要付费才能参与竞价。不得不说，这个团队在很长一段时间里都做得非常出色。事实上，这是一个典型的"用灵活方法实现增长"的案例。他们做得很棒，但当我加入团队时，公司规模和阶段已经超出了这种模式的适用范围。团队也清楚这一点。这显然是一种高摩擦的体验。用户兴致勃勃想雇人，结果却被告知"稍后联系你"，这显然不是理想的体验。（00:30:06） 更糟糕的是，你还要让供应方花钱才能出现在用户面前。用户真正需要的是直观的信息——"告诉我能雇佣谁"。但这方面存在诸多摩擦，某些情况下甚至存在不公平的营收模式。比如，服务商付费展示信息，但用户意向不强，最终既花了钱又没收获利润，形成恶性循环。（00:30:40） 因此，我们最重要的举措是重建整个增长闭环，调整盈利模式，构建一个让专业服务商能够即时报价的系统。莱尼，我相信你也清楚
爱彼迎（Airbnb）大家应该很熟悉，从需求到预订，再到即时预订的转变。这在服务和供给的不同领域里其实有着相似的逻辑。但要在数千个市场上实现这种转变，并找到合适的变现节点——何时收费、收取多少费用等——这才是Thumbtack真正扭转增长引擎的核心所在。这充分证明了创始人们的远见卓识，他们敢于突破常规，克服重重困难才取得了这样的成果。虽然我不再了解Thumbtack的具体业务细节（即便知道也不会随意透露），但据我所知，公司目前发展态势良好，相信这种策略对其发展大有裨益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, as you were talking about that, that's exactly an experience Airbnb went through. I actually led that effort at Airbnb. It took three years of my life.
turns.zh: 是啊，你刚提到这点，Airbnb就经历过这样的过程。实际上，我在Airbnb负责过这项工作。那耗费了我整整三年的时间。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Oh my gosh, we should talk about that one day.
turns.zh: 天哪，我们改天应该好好聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've written about it here and there, but honestly very quietly is one of the biggest transformations Airbnb went through, shifting from I'm going to go request a book to basically every book now on Airbnb is instant. And that was a very difficult and painful journey. But looking back, I don't think Airbnb would've made it if not for that. And unlike Thumbtack, we did it before things were starting to fall apart. And actually, I was going to say the lens that we used that I find really helpful here is, you should be asking yourself, "If somebody was to come into our space and disrupt us and start now to become the new Airbnb, what would they do?"
turns.zh: 是啊，我偶尔会写到这方面，但说实话，我一直比较低调地处理这件事。这是Airbnb经历过的最大变革之一，从“我要去请求预订”到现在Airbnb上的每本书都实现了即时预订。这是一段非常艰难而痛苦的历程。但回过头来看，如果没有这段经历，Airbnb可能就无法走到今天。与Thumbtack不同的是，我们是在一切开始分崩离析之前就完成了转型。实际上，我想说我们采用的策略非常有用——你应该问自己：“如果有人要进入我们的领域并颠覆我们，现在就成为新的Airbnb，他们会怎么做？”

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it was obvious that it'd be be make it instant, just the way it works. Welcome to Airbnb disruptor. And so, yeah.
turns.zh: 很显然，必须让它即时化，就像现在这样运作。欢迎来到Airbnb颠覆者时代。所以，是的。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Another learning there is any product you work on that involves bits and atoms is exponentially harder than products that just involve bits. But it's amazing how something as seemingly simple as make an instant ends up being so incredibly deep and complicated. And especially on an existing business, making that transition while still growing is just very, very complicated. Fantastic learning I'm sure you had as well.
turns.zh: 另一个经验是，任何涉及“比特与原子”的产品，都比仅涉及“比特”的产品难得多。但令人惊讶的是，一个看似简单的“即时化”最终却变得极其深刻和复杂。尤其是在现有业务中，边增长边完成转型实在是太难了。我相信你也一定有过类似的深刻体会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very difficult to change people's expectations and behavior. This could be its own podcast episode, just changing marketplaces into an instant experience. (00:33:14): I wanted to circle back real quick to the first lesson you had there, which is adding new channels. I think this is a really interesting takeaway here. So essentially Thumbtack was reliant on SEO. Google slash the sword, as you described, started changing things so traffic stopped coming. I think a cool lesson here is just if you're reliant on one growth channel, which I think most companies actually are, I think most companies have one main driver, I think a lesson here is potentially before things start to fall apart, especially if you're SEO-driven, start to explore more practically paid referrals.
turns.zh: 要改变人们的期望和行为实在太难了。这本身就可以单独做一期播客，专门讨论如何将市场平台转变为即时体验。（00:33:14）：我想快速回顾一下你提到的第一个教训——增加新渠道。这个观点真的很有启发。所以本质上，Thumbtack依赖于SEO。正如你所描述的，谷歌削减了流量，导致流量逐渐枯竭。我认为一个很棒的教训是，如果你依赖于一个增长渠道（我认为大多数公司实际上都是如此），你应该尽早探索更多付费引流方式，尤其是在SEO驱动的增长渠道开始崩溃之前。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Totally. I mean I think maybe it's, again, it's kind of living through that. Now, anytime I look at a product or look at a team, it's one of the first things that perks up the paranoia of just like, "Oh no. You don't want to be in that situation. Let's figure out now how you start to diversify because you just never know, like you say, when one of those might dry up."
turns.zh: 完全同意。我觉得这可能是因为亲身经历过这些。现在，每当我看待一个产品或一个团队时，这就是首先会引发警觉的事情之一。“哦，不。你们可不想陷入那种境地。现在就想办法开始多元化吧，因为你永远不知道，什么时候其中一个渠道会枯竭。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Imagine a place where you can find all your potential customers and get your message in front of them in a cost-efficient way. If you're a B2B business, that place exists, and it's called LinkedIn. (00:34:20): LinkedIn ads allows you to build the right relationships, drive results, and reach your customers in a respectful environment. Two of my portfolio companies, Webflow and Census, are LinkedIn success stories. Census had a 10X increase in pipeline with a LinkedIn startup team. For Webflow, after ramping up on LinkedIn in Q4, they had the highest marketing source revenue quarter to date. With LinkedIn ads, you'll have direct access to and can build relationships with decision makers including 950 million members, 180 million senior execs, and over 10 million C-level executives. You'll be able to drive results with targeting and measurement tools built specifically for B2B. In tech, LinkedIn generated 2 to 5X higher return on ad spend than any other social media platforms. Audiences on LinkedIn have two times the buying power of the average web audience, and you'll work with a partner who respects the B2B world you operate in. Make B2B marketing everything it can be and get $100 credit on your next campaign. Just go to linkedin.com/podlenny to claim your credit. That's linkedin.com/podlenny. Terms and conditions apply. (00:35:29): Is there anything else from your time at Thumbtack that stands out as an interesting lesson or takeaway that you bring with you to the work you do now?
turns.zh:
想象一个能帮你找到所有潜在客户，并以高性价比方式将信息传递给他们的平台。如果你是一家B2B企业，这个平台确实存在——它叫做领英。（00:34:20）：领英广告能助你建立正确的客户关系、推动业务成果，并在尊重的环境中触达目标客户。我的两家投资组合公司Webflow和Census都是领英成功案例。Census在领英启动团队的助力下，销售线索增长了10倍。Webflow在第四季度加大领英投放后，实现了迄今为止最高的营销收入来源。借助领英广告，你将直接接触到包括9.5亿会员、1800万高管和1000多万C级高管在内的决策者，建立联系。专为B2B打造的定向与数据分析工具将助你达成营销目标。在科技领域，领英的广告ROI比其他社交媒体平台高出2至5倍。领英受众的购买力是普通网络用户的两倍，而且你的合作伙伴会充分尊重你所处的B2B领域。充分发挥B2B营销的潜力，下次广告投放即可获得100美元信用额度。访问linkedin.com/podlenny即可领取。条款与条件适用。
（00:35:29）：在Thumbtack的经历中，有没有什么经验或教训特别值得分享，影响到你现在的工作？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I would say this, I think especially at the leadership level, the team that reports to the CEO, that group doesn't always have the opportunity to do a lot of project work together, right? You've got your CFO, you've got your head of sales, you've got your product and your engineering. There's just not as often as natural ways for that group to work together. And then when something happens like growth goes negative, that group is very important. And that group's ability to tackle hard things together is very important. I think that one important lesson from that is, no one can be a bystander on product strategy. Just because you've got product in your title doesn't mean you're the only one that should be thinking about product strategy certainly at that level. Certainly not in engineering. (00:36:39): The CFO, the head of people, everyone needs to have a seat at the table when it comes to product strategy, what the company's doing and what they're going to do to grow out of the situation that they're in. Because otherwise, in those hard times it can kind of be like a, "What have you done for me lately?" sort of a dynamic. And that's just not the right dynamic to have on that team. I'm not saying that at Thumbtack we had the right dynamic, but I think it was a really important learning in that moment of how that team, even if they didn't typically get as involved in things like product strategy and what we're building, how everyone had to be all hands on deck and really thinking about those sorts of problems because it's the only way I think you can get a whole company and team out of those situations by everyone getting involved in doing their part and pulling on the levers that they have in their area in order to do that well. I don't think it can work in any other way.
turns.zh: 我认为，尤其是高层团队，即向CEO汇报的团队，成员们往往没有太多机会一起开展项目工作。比如CFO、销售负责人、产品和工程团队。自然合作的机会并不多。而当遇到业务下滑时，团队的凝聚力就显得尤为重要。共同应对挑战的能力至关重要。从中得到的重要启示是，产品战略绝不是旁观者的角色。即使你的头衔里有“产品”二字，也不意味着你能独自主导产品战略，尤其是在工程团队层面。（00:36:39）：CFO、人力资源主管等成员都应参与产品战略决策，了解公司现状及未来发展方向。否则，在困境中很容易出现“你为我做了什么”的互相指责局面。这绝非团队应有的状态。我不说Thumbtack的团队做得完美，但那次经历让我深刻认识到，即便团队成员平时不常参与产品战略等事务，关键时刻也必须全员行动，共同思考问题。这是让整个公司和团队走出困境的唯一途径——通过每个人各司其职，充分发挥各自领域的优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's a lesson there. Build a relationship with the leadership team before things start to go awry.
turns.zh: 所以这里有个教训：在问题恶化之前，就要与领导团队建立良好的关系。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: That, yes. Certainly that, but I think it's also incumbent for people in our roles and engineering roles to bring strategy to that discussion, to that group, in a way that it is possible for everyone to engage and everyone to internalize and understand what it means for their area and to even have obviously a say in because they're on the leadership team at the end of the day. They should feel like their fingerprint is also on the company strategy, and as soon as it starts to feel like that's their world, that's our world. And I think that's true for any of the functions. It's true for what's happening in sales, it's true for what's happening in marketing. As product managers, we naturally need to be the connective tissue across all of that, but I think the whole leadership team at that level should feel like connective tissue across all of those functions.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。但我认为，我们这些担任管理和工程职务的人也有责任为这场讨论、为这个团队注入战略思维，让每个人都能参与其中，理解这对他们所在领域意味着什么，甚至能在其中发挥作用——毕竟他们毕竟是领导团队的成员。他们应该感受到自己的指纹也印在公司战略之上。一旦他们开始把这视为自己的事业，那就是我们的事业。我认为这对任何职能部门都适用。这适用于销售部门，适用于市场营销部门。作为产品经理，我们自然需要成为所有这些部门的连接纽带，但我认为整个领导团队都应该感觉自己是所有这些职能部门的连接纽带。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's transition to Facebook. This is I think an example of 0 to 1. So when you were at Facebook, you built what is called the New Product Experimentation team. I actually thought it was called the New Product Experiment Experience team, but I think it's New Product Experimentation team. My understanding is the idea there is, instead of Facebook having to buy the next Instagram and WhatsApp and all the things basically incubate startups within Facebook in a stabled concept, a startup within a startup, create all these startups within a startup. And as an outsider, it feels like it was really fun for a while, but it hasn't let any amazing new businesses for Facebook. Correct me if I'm wrong. I'm curious what that experience was like, what you took away from it, how it went, what you think about when you look back at that part of your journey.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来转到Facebook的话题。我认为这是一个从0到1的例子。你在Facebook的时候，组建了一个叫做“新产品实验团队”的团队。我原本以为它叫“新产品实验体验团队”，但后来确认是新产品实验团队。据我了解，这个团队的理念是，Facebook不必去收购下一个Instagram和WhatsApp之类的公司，而是要在Facebook内部孵化初创企业——可以说是在稳定的框架内创建初创企业，初创企业中的初创企业。作为局外人来看，这个模式一度很有趣，但并没有为Facebook催生出任何令人惊叹的新业务。如果我理解有误，请纠正我。我很好奇你在这段经历中的感受、从中获得的收获、项目的进展，以及回顾这段历程时你的感悟。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I was one of the few folks that kind of joined that team early and help build that team. How it ended up and how it closed down, I am not familiar with because I wasn't there. But I think in terms of was it a success or not because it didn't build the next Instagram I think is a little bit of the wrong bar to set for things like that. To some extent, it's like, "Did the group win the lottery or not? And let's judge there. Let's judge their success." Obviously I'm not saying that discovering something like Instagram is just winning the lottery, but you get what I mean in terms of the rarity of those sorts of discoveries and those sorts of products. (00:40:12): I think that that team was very realistic about what I would say would be the champagne level outcomes and/or more like the kind of beer, nice dinner kind of level outcomes.
turns.zh: 我是少数早期加入这个团队并帮助建立这个团队的人之一。我不清楚它最后是如何结束和关闭的，因为我当时不在场。但我认为判断它是否成功，不应该以是否诞生下一个Instagram为标准。某种程度上，这就像在问：“这个团队是中了彩票还是没中？然后根据这个结果来判断他们的成功。” 显然，我不是说发现像Instagram这样的产品就等于中了彩票，但你懂我的意思——这类发现和产品实在太罕见了。（00:40:12）我认为那个团队对所谓的“香槟级别”成果，或者更像是“啤酒加美味晚餐”级别的成果，有着非常务实的预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your wine.
turns.zh: 你的葡萄酒。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, the wine. Yeah, thank you. That's a better analogy. I think we built knowing those sorts of outcomes would also be very beneficial to the organization. So as an example, one of them is, at Facebook scale, doing things that don't scale or doing things that start out small was just a muscle that was really hard to come by, right? It's like any community product that you build, any kind of social where there's community density that's important early on, any product that you build that way, starting with a million users is a really hard way to do that. At places like Facebook and Google, it's like it's hard to run an experiment with a hundred people. It's not hard, it's impossible, right? And so this idea that you would have to get real small, that you would have to start very targeted, that you would have to start with things that clearly don't scale and don't have a chance of being big from the get-go is really, really hard in an organization like that. (00:41:47): And so creating that space for NPE to be able to do that, to be able to help remind the organization what are the mechanisms we need to be able to build and learn that way was very beneficial. Even simple things. At an organization of Facebook size, maybe experiences at an Airbnb, it is really hard for product managers, engineers and designers to talk directly with customers. It is basically impossible. You're almost always talking through some third party, some recruiting agency and getting reports and you're not always in the room. Imagine building a startup, like a product from day one and not being able to sit right next to your customer and being like, "Show me how you do this or show me how you do that.' It's incredibly hard. You're looking for such faint signal. (00:42:48): The idea that you would try to get it through layers of indirection and games of telephone is crazy, but at that scale, that's what you have to do because there's all of these legal concerns and many other realistic concerns about what you can say to who and who you can talk to and what you can tell them about what you're doing and all of these things. So creating an environment where those sorts of constraints were lifted and were different was very beneficial, I think, to the organization and started to shed a light on some of the things that were broken that make it hard to build 0 to 1 in those sorts of environments. (00:43:31): I also think it was a really fantastic recruiting tool. It did build a really great group of folks, many of which have left to go start interesting companies. Even if you set that light on the hill to be like, "Go find the next Instagram," many of the things that you would do along the way to find the next Instagram end up being very beneficial to the broader organization. We saw a lot of that in PE.

（00:43:31）我还认为这是一个极好的招聘工具。它确实组建了一支非常优秀的团队，其中许多人离开后创办了有趣的公司。但我想说的是，当你是一位组织领导者时，施雷普当时就是支持NPE的组织领导者，他做得非常出色，成功地为这个团队建立了隔离墙。我认为你会设定一系列目标，寻找帮助公司和组织的方法。即使你树立一个远大目标，比如“去找到下一个Instagram”，但在寻找下一个Instagram的过程中，你所做的许多事情最终也会对整个组织大有裨益。我们在NPE就看到了很多这样的例子。

turns.zh: 对于那些想在公司内部创办初创公司的人——很多大公司都在尝试这样做——你有什么建议能帮助他们取得成效吗？或许目标不一定要是打造下一个大型商业项目。还有其他子目标。你能想到什么吗？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: God, there's so many. Schrep did a really fantastic job of removing a lot of these constraints. So one is I would say think really hard about the incentive system. Smart, good people, even if they're not trying to, they end up kind of gaming things towards the incentive system. And so think long and hard about that. So for instance, if you're a large organization and you do some performance management process like twice a year and that's how you're going to evaluate and incentivize people in your 0 to 1 incubator, you've already killed it. It's the wrong incentive, it's the wrong timeframe. It creates adverse selection, problems for the sort of people that you bring in. And so it's hard in an existing organization to say, "We're going to take all these company processes around even how we level people and pay them and motivate them. And we're going to throw them out the window for this group." (00:47:27): How you build the infrastructure you use, this is something that the NP team did really well. Everyone got to do their own thing from an infrastructure perspective. Just do what is best for the problem you're trying to solve in this moment, knowing that you're likely going to throw away a lot of this code anyway. Being able to do that in an organization like Facebook or Google, if you ask anyone that works on those things, is really hard. It takes someone like a Schrep to be like, "Nope, they're going to get to do this. Sorry." And so I think that's really helpful. (00:48:01): For what it's worth, one of the organizations that we talked to that I felt like was doing this in one of the best ways was Nike. Nike has this incubation lab. It's a completely different operating model. They recruit a completely different type of person, very different incentive system. And essentially, where they end up plugging them into Nike is that when they have something into the distribution marketing kind of growth arms of Nike. But for the product discovery process, they're doing their whole different thing. Once they find some fit, then kind of Nike comes in and goes, "Boom. I'm going to help you explode your fit." But I think that the number one thing I would think about would be the incentive system and the adverse selection that that can cause.
turns.zh: 天哪，太多了。施雷普在消除这些限制方面做得非常出色。所以我要说的是，好好考虑一下激励机制。聪明优秀的人，即便他们无心为之，也会想方设法利用激励机制来谋取利益。因此，请深思熟虑这一点。比如，如果你是一家大型机构，每年进行两次绩效管理评估，并以此作为0到1孵化器中评估和激励员工的依据，那你就已经把事情搞砸了。这是不恰当的激励方式，时间框架也不合适。它会导致逆向选择，给你引入的人才带来问题。要在现有组织中推行这些改革，比如彻底抛弃现有的人员晋升、薪酬和激励体系，实在太难了。（00:47:27）：在基础设施建设方面，NP团队做得非常出色。从基础设施角度来看，每个人都可以自由发挥。只要能解决当下问题，就大胆尝试，知道最终可能大部分代码都会被废弃。在Facebook或谷歌这样的公司，能做到这一点的人可不多。这需要像施雷普这样的人站出来，说：“不行，他们必须这么做。对不起。”我认为这真的很有帮助。（00:48:01）：就我所知，我们接触过的组织中，做得最出色的当属耐克。耐克有一个孵化实验室。这是一个完全不同的运营模式。他们招募的是完全不同类型的员工，建立了截然不同的激励体系。最终将这些团队整合到耐克的分销和营销部门。但在产品创新过程中，他们又采取了完全不同的策略。一旦找到合适的方向，耐克就会介入，说：“哇哦，我们要助你一臂之力。”但我认为最关键的还是激励机制，以及由此引发的逆向选择问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky

turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我们聊聊最后一个部分——Grammarly，你们现在正处于这个阶段。在我看来，Grammarly就像一枚一级火箭，或者是二级火箭，或者……十级火箭？虽然它比一级火箭更先进，但你们目前正处于这个阶段。Grammarly让我感兴趣的地方在于，它是极少数成功的B2C订阅业务之一，几乎没有其他类似的案例。除了Duolingo和Grammarly，还有谁呢？我知道你们也在做B2B业务，但这类成功案例实在太少了。太多创业者试图在消费者订阅模式的基础上构建业务，最后却以失败告终。所以我很好奇，Grammarly目前的运营状况如何？进展如何？你们认为它能持续成功的关键因素是什么？又有哪些经验教训？虽然你加入不久，但到目前为止，你从这段经历中获得了哪些启发？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: We don't talk about it often, but Grammarly is a much bigger company from a revenue perspective than I think people realize. The company has been around for 15 years and was profitable from day one, and continues to be quite profitable. So it's a very, very healthy business that is much larger than folks might realize. And that is actually quite intentional because the company was trying not to be noticed for a long time, very intentionally. The fact that you would have grammar and spell checking in Google Docs or grammar and spell checking in Word. People would often write off the company that like, "How is that a business? How is that a feature? These products already have it." And that was very convenient for Grammarly because they could kind of navigate between these giants in tech and grow a very phenomenal business on this use case that people had written off. (00:51:30): Now, come the advent of LMS, it's no longer a use case that people are writing off and sort of the dream of the founders that machines can assist us in communication in this way that they've had for 15 years, I feel like now the whole industry is like, "Well, this is obviously how we're going to communicate and machines are going to do all these things for us." And Grammarly is now sort of in the center of that hurricane. And again, I think it's a similar thing where it's like, "Well, there's ChatGPT. There's Microsoft Copilot. How is Grammarly going to have a chats?" But yet things still seem like there's the future. The future is bright. (00:52:14): And so to your question, I think what has made it work, I've only been here for 10 months so please kind of take this with a grain of salt, but my instinct is that people really love Grammarly because of how it works and where it works. And what I mean by how it works is Grammarly is one of the few products where you just install it and it makes you better. You don't have to configure it, you don't have to manipulate it, you don't have to change anything about what you're doing. You carry on and across all of your applications, across all of your tabs, you'll start getting pushed assistance to you in the right moment. You could ignore it if you want, no big deal, but it takes a very, very small amount of effort to tap on one of those things, get some value and keep going. (00:53:04): I think that a product that is that easy to use, that easy to extract value from, but then also that prevalent, how many different text boxes do you write in a given day? I mean, it is not less than 10, it is tens or potentially hundreds, right? And so it is everywhere and it is very, very low effort to get real value from it. And then the where we work is what I said, you don't have to change anything about your workflow. Grammarly meets you where you are and you get value from it. Doing that really well at this level of quality for a user base of this scale, essentially it's like a huge AI achievement masquerading as a little UX innovation, right? But that experience, that UX that sort of brings AI to the masses has obviously served Grammarly really well. I think those are some of the strengths that we're going to continue to lean on to now provide a very different type of assistance and value that we can because of where the technology has moved.
turns.zh:
我们不常谈及此事，但从营收角度来看，Grammarly是一家比人们想象中规模大得多的公司。这家成立15年的公司从创立之初就实现盈利，且至今保持着高盈利水平。因此，它是一家极其健康的企业，其规模远超公众想象。这种低调策略实属有意为之——该公司长期刻意保持低调，避免引人注目。例如，当你使用Google Docs或Word时，能看到语法与拼写检查功能。人们常不屑地说：“这怎么能算业务？这不过是基础功能罢了。”但这种低调策略反倒为Grammarly带来了巨大机遇，让它能在科技巨头夹击中稳步发展。

随着LMS（学习管理系统）的兴起，这项被忽视的应用场景如今已成为行业共识。创始人15年前就怀揣的愿景——让机器以智能方式辅助沟通——如今正被整个行业接纳。Grammarly正处于这场技术革命的核心位置。面对ChatGPT、微软Copilot等竞争对手时，人们不禁疑问：Grammarly如何在聊天场景中立足？但未来机遇依然广阔。

回到你的问题，我认为Grammarly的成功核心在于产品易用性与场景适配性。作为仅需一键安装就能提升用户效率的产品，Grammarly无需复杂配置，用户无需更改使用习惯。无论是在何种应用场景、何种标签页下，系统都能在恰当时机提供智能协助。用户可以选择忽略提示，但轻点按钮即可获取价值，继续高效工作。

（00:51:30）：回到你的问题，我认为成功的关键在于产品设计与用户场景的完美契合。我在这里仅工作10个月，所以请谨慎看待我的观点，但我的直觉是，用户真正喜爱Grammarly是因为其易用性和实用性。所谓易用性，指的是用户无需繁琐配置，直接安装即可提升效率。无需更改使用习惯，只需在所有应用和标签页中使用，系统就能在恰当时机推送协助。用户可以选择忽略提示，但轻点按钮即可获取价值，继续高效工作。

（00:53:04）：我认为这种易用性、高价值且普及度极高的产品，日均使用次数极高。人们每天使用多个文本框进行输入，数量绝不低于10个，甚至可能达到数十或数百个。因此，Grammarly无处不在，获取价值的成本极低。至于使用场景，正如我所说，用户无需改变工作流程，Grammarly会主动适应现有环境，提供价值。在如此大规模的用户群体中实现如此高水准的AI体验，本质上是以小型UX创新伪装的大型AI成就。这种将AI带入大众视野的用户体验，无疑为Grammarly的发展注入了强劲动力。随着技术进步，我们将继续依托这些优势，为用户提供全新的协助与价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing I've heard a lot about Grammarly, and Yuri was on the podcast and who led growth for a long time at Grammarly, is just how scrappy the business has been and the founders have been from the beginning, the fact that they've been profitable from the beginning. That feels like one of the threads through all of the successful consumer subscription companies, is super scrappy, not raising money for a long time. Is there anything there that you found to be really interesting or helpful for other folks that are maybe building the space?
turns.zh: 关于Grammarly，我听说了很多相关故事。尤里曾在播客中分享，他长期负责Grammarly的增长业务，谈到这家公司从一开始就秉持着极其拼搏的精神，创始人从一开始就坚持盈利模式。我认为这正是所有成功的消费者订阅公司共同的特质——极其拼搏，长期不融资。您是否发现了什么对其他正在这个领域创业的人真正有趣或有帮助的经验？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: When you're a team that kind of starts out of Ukraine and you're not thinking that there's any chance that you're going to raise money and why would you do that, I mean it really... Back to our previous conversation of what happens when growth goes negative, it really forces you to focus on the important things. And so, like many of the early engineers who are still here because the company has done so well over the years, they think in like, "How is this work going to translate into revenue?" They think about the impact on the business from even very deep technical work that they're doing because I think they were brought up in this culture where the business doesn't really invest ahead of its profitability because it was a bootstrap business from day one. So that enforces everyone to think about their projects and their prioritization and how is what they're doing over the next two months going to actually turn into more revenue and keep the company growing and sustaining. So I think that culture is prevalent and help Grammarly get to where it is. (00:56:00): Now, I just want to be really honest that in moments that we're in like today, that can also be detrimental because the business gets to a certain size, you start getting to law of large numbers. You need to start thinking about are there other products? Are there other use cases? Are there other channels of growth? How do you invest ahead of some of that growth and start to diversify? Because at the scale and size that we are and aspire to be, we're going to have to do many more things and service many more different types of customers. And as you mentioned, we're going to have to pull off the motion of B2C to B, kind of get that product-led sales motion going. So all of those things are happening. And thankfully the business is as strong as it is where we can invest ahead now in those things while still maintaining profitability and a really strong business.
turns.zh: 当一个团队从乌克兰起步时，他们从未想过能筹集到资金，也不明白为什么要这么做。回到我们之前讨论的增长负向的情况，这实际上迫使团队专注于重要事项。比如，许多至今仍在公司的早期工程师都会思考：“这项工作如何转化为收入？”他们会审视自己正在进行的技术工作，思考其对业务的影响，因为他们深受一种文化的影响——即公司从一开始就坚持在盈利前先专注于增长。因此，每个人都必须仔细评估项目优先级，思考未来两个月的工作如何能转化为更多收入，推动公司持续增长。我认为这种文化正是Grammarly成功的秘诀。（00:56:00）：现在，我必须诚实地说，当我们像今天这样处在某个阶段时，这种文化也可能带来负面影响。当公司规模达到一定程度后，就必须遵循大数法则。需要思考是否有其他产品、用例或增长渠道？如何在增长前进行投资并实现多元化？因为以我们当前和期望的规模，我们需要开展更多业务，服务更多不同类型的客户。正如你所提到的，我们需要从B2C模式转向B2B模式，推动产品主导型销售模式的落地。所有这些工作都在进行中。幸运的是，公司目前依然强劲，我们可以在保持盈利的同时，提前布局这些战略方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing that they're still team members and maybe I think you said engineers from the beginning, 12 years later. I think that says a lot about the business. And before we started recording, they're based in Ukraine and you were saying that they're going to Zooms, there's bombs going off, they have to go into bomb shelters and then jump on a meeting. It's incredible that team continues to operate and the business continues to do this well in spite of all that.
turns.zh: 令人惊叹的是，12年后，他们仍是团队成员，甚至可能是最初的工程师。这充分说明了这家公司的文化内涵。在我们开始录制之前，他们提到公司位于乌克兰，面对炸弹袭击，工程师们不得不躲进防空洞，之后又迅速投入会议。这支团队在如此恶劣的环境下依然坚持工作、推动业务发展，实在令人钦佩。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, the team in Ukraine at Grammarly is... I mean, it's something else. It's a really fantastic team. When you speak to many of them, I think actually the work provides sometimes a very useful distraction, but they obviously feel a lot of pride in the business. They built a lot of this business. There aren't yet many businesses of this size that kind of come from Ukraine. I think that that team is incredible and continues to deliver a ton of impact to the company even in the circumstances that they're in. I know for the founders, a lot of why they want Grammarly to succeed and be the generational company that it can be is for Ukraine, and especially in this moment and it's awesome to see how that motivates them and 15 years on the same project is not nothing. That's some serious resilience. And so I think even in moments like that, using them as a way to motivate and strive for something greater I think says a lot about the founders and the team in Ukraine.
turns.zh: 是的，乌克兰的Grammarly团队……我得说，这支团队真是非同凡响。和他们中的许多人交谈时，我发现工作有时能提供一种非常有效的解压方式，但显然他们对公司充满自豪感。他们为这项事业付出了诸多心血。像Grammarly这样源自乌克兰的企业规模尚属罕见。我认为这个团队太了不起了，即便身处当下这种境遇，他们仍能为公司持续创造巨大价值。我知道创始人之所以希望Grammarly能成功，成为能延续百年的传奇企业，背后的动机很大程度上是为了乌克兰，尤其是当下这个关键时刻。看到这种激励人心的力量真是令人惊叹，坚持15年专注于同一项目绝非易事。这份韧性实在令人敬佩。因此，即便在困难时刻，借助这样的团队来激励自己、追寻更远大的目标，这足以说明创始人和乌克兰团队的非凡品质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Hopefully there's a happy resolution soon there. I don't know if you know this, I was actually born in Ukraine.
turns.zh: 没错。希望局势能尽快好转。我不知道你是否了解，我其实出生在乌克兰。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哇哦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know Odessa.
turns.zh: 我去过敖德萨。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Oh, nice.
turns.zh: 哦，不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't want to talk about that much, but it's true. And I just realized we both have skys in our last name. Lovinsky and Rachitsky.
turns.zh: 我不想多谈这个，但确实如此。我刚意识到我们姓氏里都有“sky”这个音节。Lovinsky和Rachitsky。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: So for what it's worth, my dad was born in Ukraine. He is from Kiev. My mom was from Lithuania, so yeah, I also have some Ukrainian background here.
turns.zh: 所以说，我父亲出生在乌克兰，来自基辅。我母亲来自立陶宛，所以没错，我也有乌克兰血统。

turns.en: All right, so Ukrainian episode.

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me zoom out a little bit and get to the final couple questions. Anything that just generally you find is really important to do well or mistakes they make. And this is a big broad question, but anything come to mind of like, "Here's something you should really try to do more of or less of?"
turns.zh: 让我稍微退一步，谈谈最后几个问题。从广义上看你的职业生涯，我很好奇你有没有什么通用建议能帮助人们拥有更成功的职业生涯。比如说，有哪些普遍认为很重要但容易出错的做法？这是个宏观问题，但你能否想到，比如，“你应该多做些什么，或者少做些什么？”

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Look, when you're thinking about career opportunities and what job to take, it's really, really hard to sniff out really well in a high degree of certainty like success. I think that having a good nose for people and the sort of people that you can be successful with is something that you can develop. What I found is I always try to prioritize putting myself in positions that are going to cause a lot of growth and learning. And growth and learning can be very painful. And you kind of got to be okay with that and go into that because on the other side of that pain I think is the promised land. (01:00:21): And that's just served me really well, is I can't necessarily predict with high degree of certainty that this thing's going to hit, but I can get a sense of the people around me and I certainly can find situations that are going to stretch me, that are going to force me to do things that I haven't done where I'm going to grow and learn significantly. And over sort of the arc of my career, I feel like that's served me well. So that's usually what I tell people, is focus on on that if you can.
turns.zh: 看吧，当你在考虑职业机会和选择哪份工作时，要准确预测成功确实很难。我认为善于识人，以及能与你共事成功的人建立良好关系，是可以培养的能力。我的经验是，我总是优先选择能带来大量成长和学习机会的职位。成长和学习可能很痛苦，但你得坦然接受这种痛苦，因为痛苦的另一端就是乐土。（01:00:21）这对我很管用，虽然我无法百分百预测某件事会成功，但我能感知身边的人，也能找到能拓展我的边界、迫使我做未曾尝试过的事、能让我显著成长和学习的环境。在我的职业生涯中，这种方法对我很有效。所以我通常会告诉人们，如果可以的话，就专注于这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. I've used this quote a number of times on this podcast, but something I always come back to is this line, "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek." I'm curious if there's something you have found about when the pain is too much, that you shouldn't pursue that. A lot of people get into these places where their mental health gets hit, their physical health is hit, they're just doing work they should not, it's too much. Is there anything there that you find it's just like, "Okay, maybe this is too much of discomfort"?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这条建议。我在播客中多次引用过这句话，但我总会回归到这句话：“你害怕的洞穴，往往藏着你追寻的宝藏。” 我很好奇，当痛苦难以承受时，有没有什么经验能让你意识到不该继续坚持？很多人陷入心理健康受损、身体健康恶化、做着不该做的工作，压力过大的境地。有没有什么时刻，让你觉得“好吧，也许这份不适实在太过分了”？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I mean, I think about a couple of things. I think in any situation you should be able to lean on one or two things that you're really strong at. That can be the foundation that keeps you going while you learn the other things. So just be wary of situations that are too net new. (01:01:44): There should be one or two important things as part of that job going into where you're like, "I got this. I know how to do this portion of it." So as an example, if you've never inherited a very large team and you work through how that works, but the product area that you're working on is one you're very familiar with what's necessary to be good in that product, whether it's really good sense of design or really good sense of analytical thinking, recommendation systems, what have you, there should be a couple of those things where you're like, "I got this. These things are going to be a stretch, but these things, I feel like I've got a handle on how to do this. I can always get better, but I feel like they're in my wheelhouse." And I think that tends to allow you to balance the pain with the areas that you already know and manage through in a more balanced and healthy way.
turns.zh: 我觉得关键在于，无论面对何种情况，都要能依托自己擅长的一两项技能。这能成为支撑你前行的基石，同时你还能在学习其他技能时保持动力。所以要警惕那些全新的挑战。（01:01:44）：新工作中应该有1-2项你擅长的事务，比如“我能胜任这部分工作”——比如接手一个庞大团队，你可能需要摸索方法，但你熟悉的产品领域，比如设计感、分析思维、推荐系统等，这些你得心应手。这样你就能在痛苦与已掌握的领域之间找到平衡，保持更健康的心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of that chart I think from flow of you want it to be challenging but not too challenging, and that's where you end up being most successful. Is there anything else, Noam, you want to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 这让我想起心流理论的图表——挑战要适中，才能达到最佳状态。诺亚，还有什么想和听众分享的吗？接下来进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, I just think that maybe going back to where we first started, Lenny, work on the things that make you happy, that fill you up. Life is short. We're all very lucky to be in this moment. There's no reason to spend time on things that don't give you energy. There's so much to do out there. I think that's the main thing I would focus on.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得还是要回归初心，做让你快乐、充实的事。人生短暂，能身处当下已是幸运。没必要在消耗能量的任务上浪费时间。外界有太多值得探索的事。我觉得这才是最该专注的重点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And even though there will be things that you have to do, I think it's important to try to find as much of that as you can because not everyone can just like, "Nah, I'm not going to do this work thing. I'm just going to go on a walk." But I think that's such an important point. And we've talked about this actually a bunch on recent podcasts of just doing this energy audit where you pay attention to what gives you energy and what doesn't and try to do more and more [inaudible 01:03:54]-
turns.zh: 太棒了。即便有些事不得不做，但尽可能寻找快乐的源泉也很重要。不是每个人都能说“不做这份工作了，我去散步吧”。但这确实是个重要观点。最近的播客里我们反复强调要进行能量审计，关注能量来源和消耗，努力增加正能量——

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... willing to do that again. With that, we reached a very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: ……愿意再次参与。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Yeah, I'm ready.
turns.zh: 好的，我准备好了。

turns.zh: 第一个问题，推荐给别人最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I'm going to cheat on this one and I'm only going to give you one. I'm only going to give you one because I don't want to cloud with any other. I recommend Build by Tony Fidel. It's just a good reminder to keep at it and do the thing that really gives you that energy because eventually you can make that incredible discovery.
turns.zh: 接下来这个问题我要偷懒，只给你们推荐一本。我之所以只推荐一本，是因为不想让其他书的光芒盖过它。推荐《Build》这本书的原因之一，是因为我妻子参与了这本书的创作。这本书由托尼·菲德尔（Tony Fidel）与她共同完成，我亲眼见证了整个创作过程。她是一位出色的作家，而托尼也从她身上学到了许多。所以我力荐这本书。最让我深有感触的是，他在取得如今推动我们工作的诸多突破前，经历了无数次失败。这也提醒我们要坚持不懈，专注于真正能激发热情的事业，最终必将迎来突破性的发现。

turns.zh: 下一个问题：你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.en: I really like For All Mankind, if you've seen that on Apple TV. And then I just finished the last season of Fargo. Every single season of that series I think is fantastic.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. For All Mankind though, last season, not as amazing a consensus that I agree with, but worth watching. (01:05:26): Next question. Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 太棒了。不过《为了全人类》最后一季的口碑没那么好，但还是值得一看。（01:05:26）：下一个问题。你有没有最喜欢的面试问题，喜欢问候选人的？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: I generally like interview questions that allow us to kind of do some work together, so I'm a little bit less on the behavioral "tell me about a time when" sort of stuff and more on the "Let's work a product problem together." It could be anything from like, "Let's design an alarm clock for children." Or lately I've been using one. "Given where technology is at, if we were to rebuild email, how might we do that?" I just feel like getting into it and getting into the details and really watching each other exercise our craft I think is really important. I have a whole podcast one time, if you're ready, about how most people don't know how to do leadership recruiting. And I feel like as I've advanced in my career, the interviews for some reason get easier and actually I can evaluate less about who I am as a product leader and whatnot. But yeah, those are the sorts of interview questions that I typically like.
turns.zh: 我通常喜欢能和候选人共同解决问题的面试题，所以我不太喜欢那种“讲讲你某次经历”的行为面试，而是更倾向于“让我们一起解决一个产品难题”。比如，“为儿童设计一款闹钟”之类的。最近我还用过一个面试题：“鉴于当前的技术水平，如果要重建邮箱，我们该如何设计？” 我觉得深入探讨细节，互相切磋专业能力非常重要。我曾做过一期播客，讲大多数人不知道如何进行领导力招聘。随着职业生涯的发展，面试反倒变得更轻松了，反而更难评估我作为产品负责人的能力之类的。但这些就是我喜欢的面试题类型。

turns.zh: 太棒了。最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.en: It's not recent, but I was a very early user of Arc and I really love Arc.
turns.zh: 虽然不是最近的，但我是Arc的早期用户，我很喜欢它。

turns.zh: 你现在用的窗口就在Arc里。我也喜欢Arc。我们节目上请过乔希（Josh）。

turns.en: Totally. I love the animation when you download something. I mean just like all of the little things. turns.zh: 还有两个问题。你有没有一句最常挂在嘴边的人生格言，无论是在工作中还是生活里，都能反复对自己说、与朋友或家人分享，并且觉得很有用的？

turns.speaker: Noam Lovinsky
turns.en: Gosh, for those that know me, this is going to share so much of my personality. I think the first thing that comes to mind is, we are meant to struggle. I just feel like through struggle is how we get better, how good things happen, how bonds form, and so I don't shy away from that kind of life experience.
turns.zh: 天哪，对了解我的人来说，这会暴露出我太多的个性了。我想首先想到的是，我们注定要经历挫折。我觉得正是通过克服挫折，我们才能变得更好，好事才会发生，友情才会产生，所以我从不逃避这种生活经历。

turns.en: I'm going to guess that you're Jewish. I'm also Jewish. That feels like a very Jewish thing to say. I love it.
turns.zh: 我猜你也是犹太人吧。我也是犹太人。这句话感觉很符合犹太人的思维。我喜欢。

turns.en: How would you guess, Lenny? It's literally written on my face. Yeah.

turns.en: Oh, man. Well, I find I misspell every word.

turns.en: I was about to say I have a product for you that can help with your spelling if you want.
